items.reason: In the 17-country WHO programme (2001–2005; ages recalled at one interview), the order varied across countries alongside how common each drug was. Among people who had used other illegal drugs by 29, cannabis had not already been used at their first other-drug use in 11.4% in the USA and 12.7% in New Zealand, against 83.2% in Japan and 77.8% in Nigeria, where cannabis was rare; these definitions include people who never used cannabis. The observed correspondence does not show that prevalence caused the order. items.finding:
The Kandel sentences do not overstate the source; the claim's overall verdict of insufficient evidence fits this unadjusted panel. Three wording points. (1) 'the abstract calls cannabis a crucial step ..., while the text says a drug does not invariably lead to the next': the body also calls marijuana a crucial step and a crucial stage (p. 913, left column). The tension is between those statements and the qualifications on p. 914, not between abstract and text. Suggested: 'the paper calls cannabis a crucial step (abstract and p. 913) but also says ...'. (2) 'These percentages were not adjusted for anything': they were not adjusted for other characteristics, but they are survey-weighted, for selection probabilities and school response, and the panel was reweighted to reproduce the time-1 marijuana frequency (note 4). 'Not adjusted for other characteristics' would be exact. (3) The four destinations in Table 1 (12 + 9 + 2 + 2) sum to 25 percentage points; the text and Figure 1 give 26%, presumably from unrounded cells. Harmless, but the claim's breakdown and its total come from different places.
All numbers from this source checked on the rendered pages. Sample: random sample of New York State public secondary school students in 18 schools, self-administered classroom questionnaires in fall 1971 and spring 1972 (5-6 months), N = 5,468 matched; usable questionnaires 8,206 at time 1 and 7,250 at time 2, so 5,468/8,206 = 66.6% (printed: 66 percent matched by self-generated codes); unmatched cases had a higher proportion of drug users (note 4). Seniors re-contacted 5-9 months after graduation (N = 985; 69% response; 60% matched), winter 1972-1973. Table 1 (cannabis at T1, N = 558): interval use legal only 19, cannabis 55 + 1 (error) = 56, pills 9 + 3 = 12 (the footnote's own example), psychedelics 5 + 4 = 9, cocaine 0 + 2 = 2, heroin 1 + 1 = 2. Legal only at T1 (N = 2,911): pills 2 + 1 error, psychedelics 1 error = 4%. None at T1 (N = 482): 1% error at pills. Table 2: cannabis in the interval 27% among current users of cigarettes, liquor and beer/wine (N >= 342) vs 2% among those who had never used any (N >= 467). The seniors' cohort: 16% moved from marijuana to other illicit drugs (p. 913). Other context: only about 2-3% of legal-only users went to other illicit drugs without cannabis (p. 913; the scan prints '2 c 3'); the Table 1 column Ns sum to 4,588, not 5,468, without explanation; the author says the sequences were similar across grades, sexes, family education and race, with data not presented (p. 914).

items.finding:
The claim presents the model correctly as showing that the patterns cannot by themselves identify a cause, not as disproving a gateway effect. Minor points: (1) 'a strong relative risk of using heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens after cannabis': the relative risk compares hard-drug use by 21 between people who had and had not used cannabis by 21 (estimation, p. 1499; results, p. 1500); the model section speaks of 'prior' cannabis initiation, but the survey figure of 24 does not require cannabis to come first, so 'among people who had used cannabis by 21' is exact. (2) '11 per 1,000, against 16' is per 1,000 people, not per 1,000 who used both, and counts hard drugs as first only when at least a year before cannabis (same-year starts are not counted), as the magnitude says. (3) The model's propensity is defined as a propensity to report drug use, so systematic under-reporting could produce the same patterns (p. 1502); a qualifier the claim could carry, not an overstatement. (4) Added after step 2 (the card's reporting issue 4, checked against pp. 1501-1502): what the paper calls the reliability of the propensity indicator is the correlation between indicator and propensity (a reliability of 0.99 is said to leave 2% of the variance uncaptured, and the text speaks of a 0.99 correlation), so the magnitude's 'liability measure of reliability 0.8' is an indicator correlated 0.8 with the liability, capturing 64% of its variance; on the usual definition its reliability is 0.64. Suggested wording: 'a liability measure correlated 0.8 with the liability (the paper's reliability 0.8)'.
All Morral numbers in the statement and magnitude were checked on rendered pages: NHSDA 1982 through 1994-A, 58,846 respondents aged 12-25, birth cohorts 1964-1982 (p. 1497); 157 vs 24 (p. 1500); 0.011 vs 0.016 (p. 1500), stated as 11 vs 16 per 1,000 people (p. 1501); OR 297 and 82 are printed data labels in Figure 4 (p. 1502), at reliabilities 0.0 and 0.8 read off the figure's axis (OR 2 at 0.99 is also in the text). No uncertainty interval is given for any model or survey estimate: confirmed. 'Not compared with a model that includes one' agrees with the authors' closing call for evidence comparing the gateway and common-factor models directly (p. 1503). Other points: the authors put the model's larger relative risk down to the tiny survey denominator (a 0.013 change could take the survey value above 190, p. 1500); younger vs older cannabis starters, survey 1.60 vs model 3.44 (p. 1500); the sentence defining order (p. 1500) uses Y_H < Y_M, the opportunity variables, where the initiation variables are meant (notational slip); the authors' policy inference that cannabis policies would have little effect on hard-drug use (p. 1503) goes further than showing that a no-effect model fits.

items.finding:
One sentence is one-sided. 'Several imaging studies and studies of self-control and decision-making found no difference in performance from comparison groups, although the review's conclusion states cognitive deficits as clear' leaves out that the same section reports large differences between people using several substances and controls on standard neuropsychological tests given outside the scanner (ref. 62), and an imaging study in which a brain metabolite tracked visuospatial and working-memory deficits (ref. 51) (p. 272). The review's evidence on cognition is mixed, not uniformly null; its 'clearly associated' (p. 272) and the conclusion (p. 273) still overstate it. Suggested: '...found no difference in performance from comparison groups, while one study found large differences on standard tests given outside the scanner; the review nevertheless calls the deficits clear'. Minor: (1) 'the DSM-IV diagnosis' - the review says the diagnosis was made historically under the DSM (pp. 269-270) without naming DSM-IV; the label is correct but the editors'. (2) 'in cross-sectional studies' is the editors' (accurate) description of refs 22, 23 and 31, which the review does not label. (3) 'Studies of self-control': the review cites one study of inhibitory control and one of decision-making.
All numbers from this source re-found on the rendered pages: up to 75% of rave attenders using several substances, average five drugs at the last rave (p. 270; ref. 12 is a cluster analysis of underground rave attenders, p. 274); 18% lifetime limited-range use at 12-17 years and 34% before age 16 (p. 271; annotations 18.3% and 34.1%, p. 274); extended-range use 2% at 12-17 and 13.5% at 18-29 called panel survey designs (p. 271), whereas the annotations describe refs 22 and 23 as separate national samples of young adults and adolescents, ref. 22 with 13.2% (p. 274); sedative-and-alcohol class 1.3% last year (p. 271). Definitions (lifetime, 1-12 months, same occasion), the difficulty of measuring simultaneous use and its study mostly in smaller high-risk samples (p. 270), removal of polysubstance dependence from DSM-5 and population research recording only frequency (pp. 269-270), the three latent-class ranges (pp. 269-271) and the authors' judgment that prevention and treatment research is underdeveloped (pp. 269, 273) are all as the claim states. The review gives no search methods and does not appraise its sources (it covers work of roughly the previous 18 months, p. 270), and the Australian figures (refs 22, 23) come from the authors' own group, which supports the claim's 'second-hand' framing. The review also notes that in older groups people reporting polysubstance use in the past 12 months are very likely to report simultaneous use (ref. 22, p. 271).

(2) 'Studies that compared people who use ecstasy with people who use no drugs therefore cannot separate ecstasy from the other drugs': the review says it is difficult to draw conclusions on MDMA from studies with non-user controls (p. 189). 'Cannot' is a little stronger than the source; 'can hardly' or 'have difficulty separating' would match. Not supported as worded: (1) 'cannabis use usually came before other illegal drugs, except where cannabis was rare': the order also broke down where cannabis use was moderate. In South Africa, where 8.5% had used cannabis by 29 (the paper calls this moderate; cross-country median 9.8%), 59.2% of people who used other illegal drugs had not used cannabis first, and in Mexico (8.0%) 48.4%. Of the 15 countries with estimates, three (Japan, Nigeria, South Africa) exceeded 50%. (2) 'Other illegal drugs came before cannabis in ...': Table 4 counts people who had not already used cannabis when they began other illegal drugs, which includes people who never used cannabis. In Japan, other illegal drug use by 29 (2.4%) exceeded cannabis use (1.6%), so at least a third of the people who used other illegal drugs (unweighted, at least 5 of 16) had not used cannabis at all by 29 (editors' calculation). Wording: 'the order depended on how common each drug was' is stronger than the paper. For the order itself the authors report a descriptive correspondence across countries, with no formal test; country also stands for culture, reporting and sampling differences the authors could not control; 'varied with' fits better. Magnitude: the Netherlands-USA contrast (odds ratio 7.4 vs 107.1 at ages 18-29) does not illustrate 'weaker where cannabis was more common'. Cannabis use by 29 was more common in the USA (57.6% at 18-29, 40.9% overall) than in the Netherlands (38.9%, 18.4%), and in older Dutch cohorts the odds ratios were far higher (1,805.9 at 30-44, 2,015.4 at 45-59). The 'weaker where more common' finding rests only on the pooled interaction (0.3).
Every number from this source was checked and is correct: 11.4% (USA, SE 1.2), 12.7% (New Zealand, SE 1.3), 83.2% (Japan, SE 10.9), 77.8% (Nigeria, SE 17.4), all in the Table 4 Total column and the text; 7.4 (1.8-30.4) and 107.1 (57.9-198.1), Table 3, ages 18-29; 0.3 (0.2-0.6) and 32.7 (8.3-129.0), Results 3.2 (prevalence scale not stated, as the claim says). The pairing is valid: in every country's Total column the Table 4 count does not exceed the Table 2 count. Unweighted 13/16 = 81.3% and 7/8 = 87.5%, against weighted 83.2% and 77.8%.
